title: Units and measurement
short: Convert without losing the order of magnitude.
concept: Physical quantities always come as a number and a unit. In SI units, length is in meters, time in seconds, mass in kilograms, and current in amperes.
formatHint: Write the answer in the format shown. You can use a comma or a point for decimals.

ladder.q: Easy start: how many meters are in 1 km?
ladder.hint: Kilo means thousand: multiply by 1000.
ladder.explanation: 1 km = 1000 m. Keep this 1000 — it comes back when you convert speed.

ladder.q: And how many seconds are in 1 hour?
ladder.hint: An hour has 60 minutes, each one with 60 seconds.
ladder.explanation: 1 h = 3600 s. With the meter from question 1, you have both pieces to turn km/h into m/s.

ladder.q: Put the two pieces together: convert 36 km/h to m/s.
ladder.hint: Divide by 3.6, the same shortcut as in the lesson example.
ladder.explanation: 36000 ÷ 3600 = 10, which is just 36 ÷ 3.6 = 10 m/s. The km became meters and the hour became seconds. You now have the most-asked conversion on the exam.

ladder.q: Now with 54 km/h. What is that in m/s?
ladder.hint: Same method as question 3: divide by 3.6.
ladder.explanation: 54 ÷ 3.6 = 15 m/s. Same formula, only new numbers. Keep this 15.

ladder.q: A speedometer reads 15 m/s. What is that in km/h?
ladder.hint: To go from m/s to km/h, multiply by 3.6.
ladder.explanation: 15 × 3.6 = 54 km/h: that's question 4 run backwards. On the exam it shows up in either direction.

title: Vectors in physics
short: Show forces and motion with direction.
concept: Draw arrows to scale, break forces into components when you need to, and pick a positive axis before you do any math.
example: A force of 10 N to the east and another of 4 N to the west.
steps: Result: R = 6 N to the east.
practice: Two forces of 7 N and 3 N point in the same direction. What's the resultant?
hint: Forces with the same direction and the same sense add up.
formatHint: Write the answer in the format shown. You can use a comma or a point for decimals.

medium.practice: Forces of 12 N to the east and 5 N to the west. What's the resultant?
medium.hint: Choose east as positive and subtract.

ladder.q: Warm-up: two forces of 4 N and 5 N both pull to the east. What's the resultant?
ladder.hint: Same direction and same sense: the forces add up.
ladder.explanation: R = 4 + 5 = 9 N to the east. Keep this 9 — you'll use it again right after.
ladder.formatHint: Include the unit and the direction (e.g. 9 N to the east)

ladder.q: The resultant of two forces in the same sense is 9 N and one of them is 5 N. What's the other?
ladder.hint: It's the sum backwards: subtract the force you know.
ladder.explanation: 9 − 5 = 4 N. You got the force from question 1 back by going the other way.

ladder.q: Now opposite senses: 9 N to the east and 4 N to the west. What's the resultant?
ladder.hint: Choose east as positive and subtract, like in the lesson.
ladder.explanation: R = 9 − 4 = 5 N to the east. The same forces as before, now fighting each other.
ladder.formatHint: Include the unit and the direction (e.g. 5 N to the east)

ladder.q: Forces of 14 N to the east and 6 N to the west. What's the resultant?
ladder.hint: East positive: subtract the force pointing the other way.
ladder.explanation: R = 14 − 6 = 8 N to the east — the lesson example with new numbers. Keep this 8.
ladder.formatHint: Include the unit and the direction (e.g. 8 N to the east)

ladder.q: 20 N to the east against a force to the west gives R = 8 N to the east. How big is the force to the west?
ladder.hint: Think backwards: 20 N minus what gives 8 N?
ladder.explanation: 20 − 12 = 8, so the force to the west is 12 N. You solved the resultant from the answer back to the start — exam style.

title: Motion
short: Link position, time, speed and acceleration.
concept: Speed measures distance per unit of time. Acceleration measures the change in velocity per unit of time. Pick the equation that holds the quantities you already know.
example: A car covers 120 m in 6 s. What's the average speed?
steps: Identify Δs = 120 m and Δt = 6 s.
practice: An object changes from 5 m/s to 17 m/s in 4 s. What's the acceleration?
hint: Divide the change in velocity by the time.
formatHint: Write the answer in the format shown. You can use a comma or a point for decimals.

medium.practice: An object goes from 4 m/s to 16 m/s in 3 s. What's the acceleration?
medium.hint: Divide the change in velocity by the time.

ladder.q: Warm-up: an object covers 40 m in 4 s. What's the average speed?
ladder.hint: v = Δs ÷ Δt.
ladder.explanation: v = 40 ÷ 4 = 10 m/s. Keep this 10 — you'll need it in a moment.

ladder.q: The object from question 1 goes from 10 m/s to 18 m/s in 4 s. What's the acceleration?
ladder.hint: a = Δv ÷ Δt: work out the change in velocity first.
ladder.explanation: Δv = 18 − 10 = 8, so a = 8 ÷ 4 = 2 m/s². You used the 10 from question 1 as the starting velocity.

ladder.q: How long does it take to cover 50 m at a speed of 10 m/s?
ladder.hint: Cover time on the triangle: Δt = Δs ÷ v.
ladder.explanation: Δt = 50 ÷ 10 = 5 s. Back to the speed from question 1, now solving for time.

ladder.q: A car covers 150 m in 10 s. What's the average speed?
ladder.hint: Divide the distance by the time, like in the lesson example.
ladder.explanation: v = 150 ÷ 10 = 15 m/s, the teacher's example with new numbers. Keep this 15.

ladder.q: The car at 15 m/s brakes and stops after 5 s. What's the acceleration?
ladder.hint: Δv = 0 − 15: watch the sign.
ladder.explanation: a = −15 ÷ 5 = −3 m/s²; the minus sign says the car is slowing down. It's the detail the exam likes to hide.
ladder.formatHint: Include the unit and the sign (e.g. -3 m/s²)

title: Newton's laws
concept: The second law turns forces into acceleration. It's the resultant force, not one force on its own, that matters.
example: What's the acceleration of a 4 kg mass under a resultant force of 20 N?
steps: Make a the subject: a = F/m = 20/4.
practice: What force accelerates 3 kg at 2 m/s²?
formatHint: Write the answer in the format shown. You can use a comma or a point for decimals.

medium.practice: What force accelerates 8 kg at 3 m/s²?

ladder.q: Warm-up: what force accelerates a 2 kg mass at 3 m/s²?
ladder.hint: F = m × a.
ladder.explanation: F = 2 × 3 = 6 N. Keep this 6 — you'll use it in a moment.

ladder.q: The same 6 N force applied to 3 kg: what's the acceleration?
ladder.hint: Cover acceleration on the triangle: a = F ÷ m.
ladder.explanation: a = 6 ÷ 3 = 2 m/s² — Newton's law run backwards. Keep this 2.

ladder.q: What force gives a 4 kg mass 2 m/s²?
ladder.hint: Multiply again: F = m × a.
ladder.explanation: F = 4 × 2 = 8 N. You're now working the formula both ways, using the 2 from question 2.

ladder.q: A 5 kg body is under a resultant force of 20 N. What's the acceleration?
ladder.hint: a = F ÷ m.
ladder.explanation: a = 20 ÷ 5 = 4 m/s². It's the lesson example with new numbers. Keep the force 20.

ladder.q: With the same 20 N force, what mass picks up 2 m/s²?
ladder.hint: Cover mass on the triangle: m = F ÷ a.
ladder.explanation: m = 20 ÷ 2 = 10 kg. You ran the whole triangle backwards to hunt down the mass — exam style.

title: Forces and friction
short: See what helps motion and what fights it.
concept: Weight points down, the normal force is the surface pushing back, and friction opposes motion or the tendency to move.
example: With g ≈ 10 m/s², what's the weight of 6 kg?
practice: If μ = 0.2 and N = 50 N, what's the friction force?
formatHint: Write the answer in the format shown. You can use a comma or a point for decimals.

medium.practice: With μ = 0.3 and N = 40 N, what's the friction force?

ladder.q: Warm-up: with g = 10 m/s², what's the weight of 2 kg?
ladder.hint: P = m × g.
ladder.explanation: P = 2 × 10 = 20 N. In question 2 we flip the formula and ask for the mass.

ladder.q: A body weighs 40 N. With g = 10 m/s², what's the mass?
ladder.hint: Cover mass on the triangle: m = P ÷ g.
ladder.explanation: m = 40 ÷ 10 = 4 kg. Keep these 4 kg — next up they're sitting on a table.

ladder.q: The 4 kg body is on a table, so N = P. With μ = 0.2, what's the friction force?
ladder.hint: First the weight of the body, then f = μN.
ladder.explanation: N = 40 N, so f = 0.2 × 40 = 8 N. You put weight and friction into one calculation.

ladder.q: An 8 kg schoolbag is on the floor. With g = 10 m/s², what's the weight?
ladder.hint: P = m × g.
ladder.explanation: P = 8 × 10 = 80 N. Keep this 80 — it closes the lesson next.

ladder.q: The schoolbag from question 4 weighs 80 N and rests on the floor with μ = 0.25. What's the friction force?
ladder.hint: On flat ground N = P; then apply f = μN.
ladder.explanation: f = 0.25 × 80 = 20 N. Weight and friction in one question, the way the exam usually asks.

title: Work, energy and power
concept: Work transfers energy when a force causes a displacement. Power tells you how quickly that energy is transferred.
example: A force of 30 N moves a box 4 m in the same direction. How much work?
steps: Because force and displacement line up, W = Fd.
practice: A motor does 600 J in 20 s. What's the power?
formatHint: Write the answer in the format shown. You can use a comma or a point for decimals.

medium.practice: A force of 50 N moves a box 6 m. How much work?

ladder.q: Warm-up: a force of 10 N moves a box 2 m. How much work?
ladder.hint: W = F × d, with force and displacement lined up.
ladder.explanation: W = 10 × 2 = 20 J. Keep this 20 — you'll use it in a moment.

ladder.q: Work of 20 J moved a body 4 m. What was the force?
ladder.hint: Cover force on the triangle: F = W ÷ d.
ladder.explanation: F = 20 ÷ 4 = 5 N. The same 20 from question 1, now solved backwards.

ladder.q: That work of 20 J was done in 2 s. What's the power?
ladder.hint: P = W ÷ t.
ladder.explanation: P = 20 ÷ 2 = 10 W. Here comes the lesson's second formula: work tied to time.

ladder.q: A force of 25 N moves a trolley 4 m. How much work?
ladder.hint: Force and displacement aligned: W = F × d.
ladder.explanation: W = 25 × 4 = 100 J, the lesson example with new numbers. Keep this 100.

ladder.q: A 20 W motor has to do 100 J of work. How long does it take?
ladder.hint: Cover time: t = W ÷ P.
ladder.explanation: t = 100 ÷ 20 = 5 s, using the work from question 4. It's power run backwards — exam style.

title: Momentum
short: Work through collisions and conserved momentum.
concept: Momentum depends on mass and velocity. In an isolated system, the total momentum stays the same before and after.
example: What's the momentum of a 2 kg ball moving at 6 m/s?
practice: A 4 kg mass has momentum 20 kg·m/s. What's the velocity?
hint: Make v the subject of p = mv.
formatHint: Write the answer in the format shown. You can use a comma or a point for decimals.

medium.practice: A 5 kg mass has momentum 35 kg·m/s. What's the velocity?
medium.hint: Make v the subject of p = mv.

ladder.q: Easy start: a 2 kg ball rolls along at 3 m/s. What's the momentum p = m·v?
ladder.hint: Multiply the mass by the velocity: 2 × 3.
ladder.explanation: p = 2 × 3 = 6 kg·m/s. Keep that formula — you'll use it in a moment.

ladder.q: Now backwards: a 4 kg trolley has momentum 20 kg·m/s. What's the velocity?
ladder.hint: Make v the subject: divide the momentum by the mass.
ladder.explanation: v = 20 ÷ 4 = 5 m/s; it's the same formula, solved for the velocity.

ladder.q: Back to the 2 kg ball, but now at twice the speed: 6 m/s. What's the momentum?
ladder.hint: Same mass, double the velocity: p = 2 × 6.
ladder.explanation: p = 2 × 6 = 12 kg·m/s: the velocity doubled and so did the momentum. New numbers next.

ladder.q: A 5 kg box slides along at 8 m/s. What's its momentum?
ladder.hint: Use p = m·v with the new numbers.
ladder.explanation: p = 5 × 8 = 40 kg·m/s. Only the exam step is left: what if the velocity changes?

ladder.q: A 1000 kg car slows from 15 m/s to 10 m/s. How much momentum did it lose?
ladder.hint: It lost 5 m/s. Apply p = m·v to that difference only.
ladder.explanation: Δv = 5 m/s, so Δp = 1000 × 5 = 5000 kg·m/s. This is the kind of math that shows up in collisions.

title: Circular motion
short: Understand radius, speed and centripetal acceleration.
concept: Even with constant speed, circular motion keeps changing direction. Centripetal acceleration points to the center.
example: A bend has v = 10 m/s and radius 20 m. What's the centripetal acceleration?
practice: If v = 6 m/s and r = 3 m, what's a_c?
formatHint: Write the answer in the format shown. You can use a comma or a point for decimals.

medium.practice: If v = 8 m/s and r = 4 m, what's the centripetal acceleration?
medium.hint: Square v and divide by r.

ladder.q: Easy start: on a bend the car does 4 m/s. What is v² (4 × 4)?
ladder.hint: Multiply the speed by itself.
ladder.explanation: v² = 16. Keep this 16 — it's the first step of the formula in the next question.

ladder.q: On that bend the radius is 2 m. Divide the 16 by 2. What's the centripetal acceleration?
ladder.hint: a_c = v² ÷ r, with v² = 16 and r = 2.
ladder.explanation: a_c = 16 ÷ 2 = 8 m/s²: you used the whole formula, with the 16 already done.

ladder.q: Another bend: v = 6 m/s and r = 2 m. What's the centripetal acceleration?
ladder.hint: Square 6 and divide by the radius.
ladder.explanation: a_c = 36 ÷ 2 = 18 m/s²: you did the squaring yourself. Bigger numbers next.

ladder.q: A bend has v = 10 m/s and radius 25 m. What's the centripetal acceleration?
ladder.hint: v² = 100. Then divide by 25.
ladder.explanation: a_c = 100 ÷ 25 = 4 m/s²: big radius, small acceleration. Now we go backwards.

ladder.q: On a roundabout, a_c = 9 m/s² and r = 4 m. What's the speed?
ladder.hint: Make v the subject: v² = a_c × r, then think about the square root.
ladder.explanation: v² = 9 × 4 = 36, so v = 6 m/s. Same formula as question 4, now solved for the speed.

title: Pressure and fluids
concept: Pressure is force spread over an area. In fluids, pressure grows with depth and depends on density.
example: A force of 200 N acts on 4 m². What's the pressure?
practice: 100 N act on 5 m². What's the pressure?
formatHint: Write the answer in the format shown. You can use a comma or a point for decimals.

medium.practice: A force of 180 N acts on 6 m². What's the pressure?

ladder.q: Easy start: 20 N acts on an area of 4 m². What's the pressure p = F/A?
ladder.hint: Divide the force by the area: 20 ÷ 4.
ladder.explanation: p = 20 ÷ 4 = 5 Pa. Keep these 5 Pa — they come straight back in the next one.

ladder.q: If the pressure is 5 Pa and the area becomes 8 m², what's the force F = p·A?
ladder.hint: Multiply the pressure by the area: 5 × 8.
ladder.explanation: F = 5 × 8 = 40 N: the same relation as question 1, now asking for the force.

ladder.q: That 40 N rests on an area of 5 m². What's the pressure?
ladder.hint: Back to the formula p = F ÷ A with the 40 N.
ladder.explanation: p = 40 ÷ 5 = 8 Pa: you've closed the force–pressure–area triangle. Bigger numbers next.

ladder.q: A force of 120 N acts on an area of 4 m². What's the pressure?
ladder.hint: Divide 120 by 4.
ladder.explanation: p = 120 ÷ 4 = 30 Pa: the classic exam case with F/A straight off. Only depth is missing.

ladder.q: In a swimming pool, ρ = 1000 kg/m³ and g = 10 m/s². What's the water pressure at 3 m deep?
ladder.hint: Use p_h = ρgh: multiply 1000 × 10 × 3.
ladder.explanation: p_h = 1000 × 10 × 3 = 30000 Pa. That's the lesson's second formula, already in exam style.

title: Heat and temperature
short: Tell thermal energy and temperature apart.
concept: Temperature describes the thermal state; heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference. Thermal capacity links energy, mass and temperature change.
example: How much heat raises 2 kg, with c = 1000 J/kg°C, by 5°C?
practice: If m = 1 kg, c = 4000 and ΔT = 2°C, what's Q?
formatHint: Write the answer in the format shown. You can use a comma or a point for decimals.

medium.practice: m = 2 kg, c = 500 J/kg°C and ΔT = 4°C. How much heat?
medium.hint: Multiply mass, specific heat and the change.

ladder.q: Easy start: the water warms from 20 °C to 30 °C. What's ΔT?
ladder.hint: ΔT is the difference: final temperature minus the starting one.
ladder.explanation: ΔT = 30 − 20 = 10 °C. Keep this 10 — you'll multiply it in question 3.

ladder.q: If m = 2 kg and c = 500 J/kg°C, how many joules raise the temperature by 1 °C?
ladder.hint: Multiply the mass by the specific heat: 2 × 500.
ladder.explanation: m × c = 1000 J for every °C. Keep the 1000: it joins the 10 next.

ladder.q: Put it all together: Q = mcΔT with m·c = 1000 and ΔT = 10 °C. What's Q?
ladder.hint: Multiply the 1000 by the 10 °C.
ladder.explanation: Q = 1000 × 10 = 10000 J. Piece by piece you built the whole formula; now with new numbers.

ladder.q: m = 3 kg, c = 200 J/kg°C and ΔT = 10 °C. What's the heat Q?
ladder.hint: Multiply the three factors: 3 × 200 × 10.
ladder.explanation: Q = 3 × 200 × 10 = 6000 J. Only the exam step is left: making ΔT the subject.

ladder.q: Heating 2 kg of water (c = 1000 J/kg°C) takes 4000 J. What's ΔT?
ladder.hint: Make ΔT the subject: divide Q by m × c.
ladder.explanation: ΔT = 4000 ÷ (2 × 1000) = 2 °C. Same formula as question 4, now solved for ΔT.

title: Electricity and circuits
short: Calculate current, voltage, resistance and power.
concept: Current is the flow of charge; voltage is energy per charge; resistance holds that flow back. In series the current is the same; in parallel the voltage is the same.
example: A 6 Ω resistor connected to 12 V. What's the current?
practice: An appliance draws 3 A at 10 V. What's the power?
formatHint: Write the answer in the format shown. You can use a comma or a point for decimals.

medium.practice: A 5 Ω resistor connected to 20 V. What's the current?

ladder.q: Easy start: a 5 Ω resistor is connected to 10 V. What's the current I = V/R?
ladder.hint: Divide the voltage by the resistance: 10 ÷ 5.
ladder.explanation: I = 10 ÷ 5 = 2 A. Keep these 2 A — you'll use them in the next one.

ladder.q: With the same 10 V and 2 A, what's the power P = V·I?
ladder.hint: Multiply the voltage by the current: 10 × 2.
ladder.explanation: P = 10 × 2 = 20 W: current first, power after, just like the exam.

ladder.q: An appliance at 20 V pulls 4 A. What's the resistance R = V/I?
ladder.hint: Divide the voltage by the current: 20 ÷ 4.
ladder.explanation: R = 20 ÷ 4 = 5 Ω — the same 5 Ω as question 1. Keep an eye out — this 5 comes back.

ladder.q: A 4 Ω resistor is connected to 20 V. What's the current?
ladder.hint: Apply I = V ÷ R: 20 ÷ 4.
ladder.explanation: I = 20 ÷ 4 = 5 A. Keep these 5 A — they're all that's left for the final power.

ladder.q: The same 4 Ω resistor at 20 V: what's the power dissipated?
ladder.hint: You already have 5 A. Use P = V·I with the 20 V.
ladder.explanation: P = 20 × 5 = 100 W (or V²/R = 400 ÷ 4). Two steps of Ohm in one question — exam style.

title: Magnetism
short: Read fields and forces in currents and magnets.
concept: Magnetic fields have direction and can push on currents and moving charges. Use the right-hand rule to find the direction of the field around a wire.
example: A wire perpendicular to the field has B = 2 T, I = 3 A and L = 0.5 m. What's the force?
practice: If B = 1 T, I = 4 A and L = 2 m, what's the perpendicular force?
formatHint: Write the answer in the format shown. You can use a comma or a point for decimals.

medium.practice: B = 2 T, I = 2 A and L = 3 m, wire perpendicular. What's the force?

ladder.q: Easy start: wire perpendicular to the field, B = 2 T and I = 3 A. What is B × I?
ladder.hint: Multiply the two values: 2 × 3.
ladder.explanation: B × I = 6. Keep this 6 — all that's left is to multiply by the length of the wire.

ladder.q: Multiply the 6 from question 1 by L = 0.5 m. What's the force F = B·I·L?
ladder.hint: The wire is perpendicular, so sin θ = 1.
ladder.explanation: F = 6 × 0.5 = 3 N. You've already used the whole formula; now with more length.

ladder.q: Same B = 2 T and I = 3 A, but now L = 2 m. What's the force?
ladder.hint: Reuse the 6: multiply by 2.
ladder.explanation: F = 6 × 2 = 12 N: doubling the length doubled the force. New numbers next.

ladder.q: A 5 m cable perpendicular to the field: B = 2 T and I = 4 A. What's the force?
ladder.hint: Multiply the three factors: B × I × L.
ladder.explanation: F = 2 × 4 × 5 = 40 N. The exam detail is still to come: a wire that isn't perpendicular.

ladder.q: A wire at 30° to the field (sin 30° = 0.5): B = 4 T, I = 5 A and L = 1 m. What's the force?
ladder.hint: Multiply B × I × L, then by 0.5.
ladder.explanation: F = 4 × 5 × 1 × 0.5 = 10 N: it was 20 N perpendicular, and the sine cut it in half.

title: Waves and optics
concept: Waves carry energy. The frequency tells you how many cycles happen each second; the wavelength is the distance between crests.
example: A wave has f = 5 Hz and λ = 2 m. What's the speed?
practice: If v = 12 m/s and f = 4 Hz, what's λ?
hint: Make λ the subject: λ = v/f.
formatHint: Write the answer in the format shown. You can use a comma or a point for decimals.

medium.practice: A wave has v = 18 m/s and f = 6 Hz. What's the wavelength?
medium.hint: Make λ the subject of v = fλ.

ladder.q: Easy start: a wave has f = 4 Hz and λ = 2 m. What is f × λ?
ladder.hint: Multiply the two values.
ladder.explanation: f × λ = 8: that's the speed of the wave. Keep this 8 — you use it next.

ladder.q: With v = 8 m/s, the frequency drops to 2 Hz. What is λ = v/f?
ladder.hint: Divide the speed by the frequency.
ladder.explanation: λ = 8 ÷ 2 = 4 m: you ran the operation the other way. The 4 carries into the next one.

ladder.q: A wave has f = 5 Hz and λ = 4 m (the one from question 2). What's the speed v?
ladder.hint: Multiply again: f × λ.
ladder.explanation: v = 5 × 4 = 20 m/s. Keep this 20 — it's the speed in question 4.

ladder.q: A wave moving at 20 m/s has frequency 4 Hz. What's the wavelength?
ladder.hint: Make λ the subject: divide 20 by 4.
ladder.explanation: λ = 20 ÷ 4 = 5 m: the same numbers as before, operation reversed. Only the kHz detail is left.

ladder.q: A sound wave has f = 0.5 kHz (500 Hz) and λ = 0.6 m. What's the speed?
ladder.hint: 0.5 kHz is 500 Hz. Multiply 500 × 0.6.
ladder.explanation: v = 500 × 0.6 = 300 m/s: that's the real speed of sound. On the exam, always convert the kHz.
